Bibliometric Review Tracks Surge in Pulmonary Embolism Artificial Intelligence Studies

A bibliometric analysis of 590 scientific publications has mapped global research trends in the application of artificial intelligence to pulmonary embolism, revealing rapid growth alongside significant limitations in clinical deployment. The study examined relevant papers published between 2006 and 2025 indexed across the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases. Researchers applied specialized bibliometric software packages, including R software, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace, to perform a visual and structural analysis of retrieved academic literature spanning two decades.

Publication trends documented by the analysis show that scholarly output developed slowly in the initial years before undergoing an exponential surge. Between 2006 and 2017, investigators identified 62 articles, representing 10.5 percent of the total volume. Output expanded rapidly from 2018 onward, culminating in 375 articles, or 63.6 percent of the corpus, published between 2023 and 2025. By 2025, annual publication volume was approximately 14 times greater than in 2017, conforming to an exponential trajectory with a coefficient of determination of 0.876.

The underlying academic network encompasses 3,844 distinct authors and 1,377 institutions across 63 countries and regions. Research production remains concentrated within a small subset of participating nations. The United States and China emerged as the two most prolific countries, producing 257 articles with 9,791 citations and 117 articles with 1,320 citations, respectively. Among the top ten most active nations, the highest average citation rates per individual article were achieved by investigators in Germany and the United States.

Keyword analysis revealed distinct thematic clusters within the broader pulmonary embolism domain. Author-selected keywords clustered predominantly around imaging modalities and diagnostic applications of artificial intelligence algorithms. Recent burst keyword analysis highlighted emerging areas of interest in research literature, with terms such as prediction and risk factors showing notable recent surges in frequency across peer-reviewed investigations.

Despite the proliferation of publications and algorithmic models, the mapping revealed significant gaps between theoretical development and practical healthcare implementation. While several artificial intelligence models achieved promising discriminative performance within single-center or few-center evaluations, the existing literature does not establish proven clinical effectiveness or verified improvements in patient outcomes. Current published investigations remain overwhelmingly focused on image-based detection rather than validated clinical decision support tools.

The study authors concluded that future progress will require addressing fundamental methodological shortcomings in the research base. Moving artificial intelligence systems into routine clinical pulmonary embolism care will depend on prospective, multicentre studies featuring rigorous external validation, as well as increased cross-national and multidisciplinary collaboration among research teams.

The clinical imperative driving this research stems directly from the global health burden of pulmonary embolism, which remains a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and death worldwide. Although a steadily expanding volume of scientific literature has explored artificial intelligence approaches for patient care, the authors observed that the global research landscape encompassing diagnosis, risk stratification, and prognostication had never previously undergone systematic mapping.

Subject of Research: Bibliometric analysis of global artificial intelligence research trends in pulmonary embolism

Article Title: Artificial intelligence in pulmonary embolism: a bibliometric analysis of global research trends and future perspectives

Article References: Xiong, T., Abulimiti, K., Zhang, Y., & Shi, L. (2026). Artificial intelligence in pulmonary embolism: a bibliometric analysis of global research trends and future perspectives. Frontiers in Medicine, 13, Article 1978579. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1978579

Keywords: pulmonary embolism, artificial intelligence, machine learning, bibliometrics, CiteSpace, VOSviewer, R software, diagnostic imaging, Web of Science, Scopus, citation analysis, risk factors, prediction models, clinical decision support, scientific publishing, multicentre validation

News Source: Blake Davidson. (November 21, 2026). Bibliometric Review Tracks Surge in Pulmonary Embolism Artificial Intelligence Studies. Scienmag.
